concepts.title: What is a Vector?
concepts.contentHtml:
A vector is a quantity with both magnitude (size) and direction.

Visually, it's an arrow pointing from one place to another. Mathematically, it's a list of numbers -- its components.

In 2D, a vector has two components: how far right/left and how far up/down.

concepts.title: Vector Addition & Scaling
concepts.contentHtml:
Adding vectors: place them tip-to-tail. The result goes from the start of the first to the end of the last. Component-wise, just add each component.

Scaling (scalar multiplication): multiply each component by a number. This stretches or shrinks the arrow.

concepts.title: Basis & Span
concepts.contentHtml:
A basis is a minimal set of vectors that can generate every vector in a space through addition and scaling.

The standard basis in 2D is î = (1,0) and ĵ = (0,1). Every 2D vector is some combination of these two.

The set of all combinations you can make is called the span. Two non-parallel vectors span all of 2D space.

concepts.title: Matrices Transform Space
concepts.contentHtml:
A matrix is not just a grid of numbers -- it's a function that transforms vectors.

A 2×2 matrix takes every point in 2D space and moves it to a new location. The entire grid of space gets warped.

To apply the transformation: multiply the matrix by a vector.
mathExpressions: \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} ax + by \\ cx + dy \end{pmatrix}

concepts.title: Common Transformations
concepts.contentHtml:
Rotation by 90°: Turns everything counterclockwise.

Reflection: Flips across an axis.

Scaling: Stretches or squishes along axes.

Shear: Slants space -- like pushing the top of a book sideways.

Each of these is represented by a specific 2×2 matrix!

concepts.title: Matrix Multiplication = Composition
concepts.contentHtml:
Applying two transformations in sequence is the same as multiplying their matrices.

If A rotates and B scales, then BA means: first apply A, then apply B.

Note the order matters! Matrix multiplication is not commutative -- AB ≠ BA in general.

concepts.title: Lines as Equations
concepts.contentHtml:
A system of two linear equations in 2D is just two lines. The solution is where they intersect.

Three possibilities:

1. One solution: The lines cross at a single point
2. No solution: The lines are parallel (never meet)
3. Infinite solutions: The lines are the same line

concepts.title: Gaussian Elimination
concepts.contentHtml:
Gaussian elimination is a systematic method for solving systems. You perform row operations on an augmented matrix to reach row echelon form.

Allowed operations:
1. Swap two rows
2. Multiply a row by a nonzero constant
3. Add a multiple of one row to another

Then back-substitute to find the solution.

concepts.title: The Determinant
concepts.contentHtml:
The determinant of a matrix tells you how much the transformation scales area.

If det = 0, the transformation squishes space down to a lower dimension -- and the system has no unique solution.

If det ≠ 0, the matrix is invertible and there's exactly one solution.
mathExpressions: \det \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc

title: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors
description: The vectors that stay on their line

concepts.title: What Are Eigenvectors?
concepts.contentHtml:
When you apply a matrix transformation, most vectors change direction. But some special vectors only get scaled -- they stay on the same line.

These are eigenvectors. The scaling factor is the eigenvalue.

"Eigen" is German for "own" or "characteristic."

concepts.title: Finding Eigenvalues
concepts.contentHtml:
To find eigenvalues, solve the characteristic equation:

Rearrange A⃗v = λ⃗v to (A - λI)⃗v = 0. For non-trivial solutions, the determinant must be zero.

For a 2×2 matrix, this gives a quadratic equation in λ.

concepts.title: Why Eigenvalues Matter
concepts.contentHtml:
Eigenvalues appear everywhere in applied math:

Stability analysis: If all eigenvalues have negative real parts, a system is stable
Google's PageRank: The ranking is the eigenvector of the web's link matrix
Quantum mechanics: Observable quantities are eigenvalues of operators
PCA: Eigenvectors of the covariance matrix give principal components

title: Abstract Vector Spaces
description: Beyond arrows -- polynomials, functions, and more

concepts.title: What Counts as a Vector Space?
concepts.contentHtml:
Vectors don't have to be arrows! A vector space is any collection of objects where you can add them and scale them, and certain rules hold.

Surprising examples of vector spaces:

• All polynomials of degree ≤ n
• All continuous functions on [0,1]
• All 2×2 matrices
• Solutions to a homogeneous linear DE

All the theorems about bases, dimension, and linear maps apply to all of these!

concepts.title: Subspaces
concepts.contentHtml:
A subspace is a vector space living inside a bigger one. It must contain the zero vector, and be closed under addition and scaling.

Key subspaces of a matrix A:

Column space Col(A): all possible outputs of the transformation A⃗v. This tells you what the matrix can "reach."

Null space Null(A): all vectors that A sends to zero. These are the inputs the matrix "ignores."

concepts.title: Dimension & the Rank-Nullity Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
The dimension of a vector space is the number of vectors in any basis (they all have the same size).

For an m×n matrix A:

Rank = dimension of the column space (how many independent directions the output covers)

Nullity = dimension of the null space (how many dimensions get squished to zero)

The beautiful Rank-Nullity Theorem: rank + nullity = n (the number of columns). Nothing is lost — every input dimension either reaches the output or gets collapsed.

title: Orthogonality & Projections
description: Perpendicularity, dot products, and least squares

concepts.title: The Dot Product
concepts.contentHtml:
The dot product of two vectors measures how much they point in the same direction.

Compute it by multiplying corresponding components and summing: (a,b)·(c,d) = ac + bd.

Key properties:

• If the dot product is 0, the vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal)
• It relates to the angle: u·v = |u||v|cosθ
• u·u = |u|² (the squared length)
mathExpressions: \vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 + \cdots + u_n v_n

concepts.title: Projections
concepts.contentHtml:
The projection of vector b onto vector a is the shadow of b cast onto the line of a.

This gives the closest point on the line of a to the tip of b.

Projections are the foundation of least squares — when a system Ax = b has no exact solution (more equations than unknowns), the best approximate solution minimizes the distance to b by projecting onto the column space of A.

concepts.title: Orthogonal Bases & Gram-Schmidt
concepts.contentHtml:
An orthogonal basis is one where every pair of basis vectors is perpendicular. This makes projections and decompositions trivially easy.

The Gram-Schmidt process takes any basis and produces an orthogonal one:

1. Keep the first vector
2. Subtract its projection from the second vector
3. Subtract both projections from the third, and so on

If you also normalize each vector to length 1, you get an orthonormal basis — the gold standard.

concepts.title: Diagonalization
concepts.contentHtml:
If a matrix A has n linearly independent eigenvectors, we can write A = PDP⁻¹, where D is a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues and P's columns are the eigenvectors.

Why is this useful? Diagonal matrices are trivial to work with:

• A² = PD²P⁻¹ (just square the diagonal entries!)
• A¹⁰⁰ = PD¹⁰⁰P⁻¹ (instant power computation)
• e^A = Pe^D P⁻¹ (matrix exponentials for DEs)

concepts.title: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
concepts.contentHtml:
Not every matrix can be diagonalized. But every matrix — even rectangular ones — has an SVD: A = UΣVᵀ.

U and V are orthogonal matrices (rotations/reflections), and Σ is diagonal with non-negative singular values.

Interpretation: every linear transformation is a rotation, then a scaling along axes, then another rotation. The singular values are the scaling factors.

concepts.title: Applications of SVD
concepts.contentHtml:
SVD is arguably the most important factorization in applied math:

Image compression: Keep only the largest singular values — a rank-k approximation uses far less storage.

PCA: Principal Component Analysis finds the directions of maximum variance via SVD of the data matrix.

Recommender systems: Netflix prize — SVD factors the user-movie rating matrix to predict missing entries.

Pseudoinverse: SVD gives the best solution to unsolvable systems.

title: Inner Product Spaces & Beyond
description: Generalized geometry and the spectral theorem

concepts.title: Inner Product Spaces
concepts.contentHtml:
The dot product is just one example of an inner product. An inner product space is any vector space with a way to measure angles and lengths.

For functions on [0,1], we define: ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫₀¹ f(x)g(x) dx

This lets us talk about "perpendicular functions" and "length of a function" — the foundation of Fourier analysis!

concepts.title: Symmetric Matrices & the Spectral Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
A symmetric matrix (A = Aᵀ) has magical properties:

• All eigenvalues are real (not complex)
• Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal
• It's always diagonalizable: A = QΛQᵀ with Q orthogonal

This is the Spectral Theorem — one of the most beautiful results in linear algebra. It says every symmetric transformation is just scaling along perpendicular axes.

concepts.title: Positive Definite Matrices
concepts.contentHtml:
A symmetric matrix is positive definite if xᵀAx > 0 for every nonzero x. Equivalently, all eigenvalues are positive.

Positive definite matrices are everywhere:

• Covariance matrices in statistics
• Hessians at minima in optimization
• Metric tensors in differential geometry
• Kernel matrices in machine learning

They represent "bowl-shaped" quadratic forms — always curving upward, with a unique minimum.

concepts.title: Generalized Eigenvectors & Jordan Blocks
concepts.contentHtml:
Not every matrix is diagonalizable -- when eigenvalues repeat, there may not be enough independent eigenvectors. The fix: generalized eigenvectors.

A generalized eigenvector of rank k satisfies (A - lambda I)^k v = 0 but (A - lambda I)^{k-1} v is not zero. These fill in the missing dimensions.

A Jordan block J_k(lambda) is a k x k matrix with lambda on the diagonal and 1's on the superdiagonal. It represents the action of A on a chain of generalized eigenvectors.

concepts.title: Every Matrix Has a Jordan Form
concepts.contentHtml:
The Jordan Normal Form Theorem states that every square matrix over the complex numbers is similar to a block-diagonal matrix of Jordan blocks:

A = P J P^{-1}, where J = diag(J_{k1}(lambda_1), J_{k2}(lambda_2), ...).

This is the "best possible" simplification when diagonalization fails. If all Jordan blocks are 1x1, you recover ordinary diagonalization.

The Jordan form is unique up to the ordering of blocks, making it a complete invariant for similarity of matrices.

concepts.title: Matrix Exponentials via Jordan Form
concepts.contentHtml:
The matrix exponential e^{tA} is essential for solving systems of linear differential equations: dx/dt = Ax has solution x(t) = e^{tA} x(0).

Computing e^{tA} directly is hard, but the Jordan form makes it tractable: e^{tA} = P e^{tJ} P^{-1}.

The exponential of a Jordan block has a beautiful pattern: e^{tJ_k(lambda)} = e^{lambda t} times a matrix with polynomial entries t, t^2/2!, ..., t^{k-1}/(k-1)! on the superdiagonals.

This explains why repeated eigenvalues produce solutions with polynomial-times-exponential growth: terms like t e^{lambda t} and t^2 e^{lambda t}.
mathExpressions: e^{tA} = P e^{tJ} P^{-1}, \quad \frac{dx}{dt} = Ax \implies x(t) = e^{tA} x(0)

concepts.title: Multilinear Maps & Tensor Products
concepts.contentHtml:
A bilinear map is a function f(u, v) that is linear in each argument separately. The tensor product V tensor W is the universal space for bilinear maps out of V x W.

The element u tensor v represents the "pure tensor" of u and v. Not every element of V tensor W is a pure tensor -- general elements are sums of pure tensors.

Key property: if V has dimension m and W has dimension n, then V tensor W has dimension mn. A basis is {e_i tensor f_j} where {e_i} and {f_j} are bases for V and W.

concepts.title: Universal Property & Basis
concepts.contentHtml:
The tensor product is characterized by a universal property: every bilinear map V x W to Z factors uniquely through V tensor W. This means V tensor W is the "freest" bilinear construction.

Key computational rules:

(u1 + u2) tensor v = u1 tensor v + u2 tensor v (linear in first argument)

u tensor (v1 + v2) = u tensor v1 + u tensor v2 (linear in second argument)

(c u) tensor v = u tensor (c v) = c (u tensor v) (scalars float freely)

These rules let you compute with tensors concretely while the universal property provides theoretical power.

concepts.title: Applications of Tensor Products
concepts.contentHtml:
Tensor products appear throughout mathematics and physics:

Quantum mechanics: The state space of a composite quantum system is the tensor product of the individual state spaces. Entanglement occurs precisely when a state is NOT a pure tensor -- it cannot be decomposed into independent subsystem states.

Differential geometry: Tensors on manifolds (like the metric tensor and curvature tensor) live in tensor products of tangent and cotangent spaces.

Machine learning: Multi-dimensional arrays ("tensors" in frameworks like PyTorch) are elements of tensor products of vector spaces, and operations like the attention mechanism involve tensor contractions.

concepts.title: Floating Point & Condition Numbers
concepts.contentHtml:
Computers use floating point arithmetic, which introduces rounding errors. A key question: when does a small error in the input cause a large error in the output?

The condition number kappa(A) of a matrix measures this sensitivity. For a square matrix, kappa(A) = ||A|| * ||A^{-1}||.

If kappa(A) is large (the matrix is ill-conditioned), even tiny perturbations in b can cause huge changes in the solution to Ax = b. If kappa(A) is close to 1 (well-conditioned), the solution is stable.

Rule of thumb: if kappa(A) is around 10^k, you lose about k digits of accuracy.

concepts.title: QR Factorization & Gram-Schmidt in Practice
concepts.contentHtml:
QR factorization writes A = QR where Q is orthogonal and R is upper triangular. It's the numerically stable way to solve least squares and eigenvalue problems.

The classical Gram-Schmidt process is mathematically elegant but numerically unstable: rounding errors accumulate and the resulting vectors lose orthogonality.

The fix is modified Gram-Schmidt: instead of computing all projections at once, subtract each projection immediately before computing the next. This simple reordering dramatically improves numerical stability.

Householder reflections provide an even more stable alternative by using orthogonal transformations to zero out columns.
mathExpressions: A = QR, \quad Q^T Q = I, \quad R \text{ upper triangular}

concepts.title: Iterative Methods: CG & GMRES
concepts.contentHtml:
For large sparse systems (millions of unknowns), direct methods like Gaussian elimination are too expensive. Iterative methods find approximate solutions that improve with each iteration.

Conjugate Gradient (CG) solves Ax = b when A is symmetric positive definite. It's guaranteed to converge in at most n steps, but in practice converges much faster when the eigenvalues are clustered.

GMRES (Generalized Minimal Residual) handles general (non-symmetric) systems. It minimizes the residual ||Ax - b|| over a growing Krylov subspace at each step.

Both methods only need matrix-vector products Av, never the full matrix. This makes them ideal for problems where A is defined implicitly (e.g., from PDEs or graph Laplacians).

title: Linear Algebra in Machine Learning
description: PCA, kernels, and the attention mechanism

concepts.title: PCA Deep Dive
concepts.contentHtml:
Principal Component Analysis finds the directions of maximum variance in data. Given data matrix X (centered), the principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix X^T X (or equivalently, the right singular vectors from SVD of X).

The classic application: eigenfaces. Treating each face image as a high-dimensional vector, PCA finds the "directions" in face-space that capture the most variation. The top eigenvectors look like ghostly faces -- they form a basis for representing and recognizing faces.

Dimensionality reduction: Projecting data onto the top k principal components captures most variance with far fewer dimensions, enabling visualization and noise removal.
mathExpressions: \text{Cov} = \frac{1}{n} X^T X = V \Lambda V^T, \quad \text{PCs are columns of } V

concepts.title: Kernel Methods & RKHS
concepts.contentHtml:
The kernel trick lets algorithms that depend only on dot products (like SVM, PCA) operate in a high-dimensional feature space without ever computing the coordinates explicitly.

A kernel function k(x, y) computes the inner product in feature space: k(x, y) = phi(x) . phi(y), where phi maps inputs to a (potentially infinite-dimensional) space.

A Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) is a function space where evaluation at a point is a continuous linear functional. Every positive definite kernel defines an RKHS, and vice versa. This provides the rigorous foundation for kernel methods.

Common kernels: polynomial k(x,y) = (x.y + c)^d, Gaussian RBF k(x,y) = exp(-||x-y||^2 / 2 sigma^2).

concepts.title: Attention as Linear Algebra
concepts.contentHtml:
The attention mechanism in transformers (the architecture behind GPT, BERT, etc.) is fundamentally a sequence of linear algebra operations.

Each token is embedded as a vector. Three linear maps produce Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices. Attention computes:

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V

The Q K^T product computes pairwise dot products (similarities) between queries and keys -- this is a big matrix multiplication. The softmax normalizes these into attention weights. Multiplying by V produces a weighted combination of value vectors.

Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel (each with different linear projections), then concatenates and linearly projects the results. The entire mechanism is a composition of matrix multiplications and a pointwise nonlinearity.
